passage: Sunday night. Papa gave me my first weekly pocket money today, fifty rupees, right in my hand like a grown-up. I felt about three metres tall 😊. I nearly ran to buy stickers with all of it. Then I thought about Papa leaving the shop late every evening and Mummy checking bills at the kitchen table. This money is their tired days. So I put twenty in my savings box. I'll spend ten on a pencil for Raghav's birthday and keep the rest for a notebook I actually need. Tomorrow I'll say thank you properly. - Vidya

qa.q: How much pocket money did Vidya receive?
What was Vidya feeling when Papa put the money in Vidya's hand, and what made Vidya think again?
qa.a: Vidya felt grown-up, then thoughtful: Vidya remembered Papa leaving the shop late and Mummy checking bills, so the money felt like their tired days.

qa.q: How could Vidya show that the pocket money is valued?
qa.a: Plan the spending, save some and buy things Vidya really needs, as Vidya's plan already does.

qa.q: How might Papa feel when Vidya thanks him properly?
qa.a: Probably proud and touched, because it shows Vidya understands the work behind the money.

grounding: Illustrates a child receiving pocket money who feels grown-up and grateful for the parents' hard work.

passage: When I turned ten, my mother, Nirmala, started giving me pocket money every Sunday: two crisp twenty-rupee notes. I'm Abhinav, and I felt so grown up, keeping them in my own zip pouch. The first few weeks I spent them on the first thing I saw, gummies and stickers. Then one night I woke at four and saw Amma coming home from her night shift at the hospital, still in her nurse's uniform, rubbing her feet at the kitchen table. I thought about my forty rupees. That Sunday, when she handed them over, I said, 'Thank you, Amma,' and actually meant it. I bought a pencil I needed and kept the rest for her birthday. When I gave her a jasmine gajra, she laughed and cried at the same time.

qa.q: How much pocket money did Abhinav get each Sunday?
What did Abhinav feel after seeing Amma come home from her night shift?
qa.a: Grateful and moved, seeing how hard she worked.

qa.q: How did Abhinav's choices change after that night?
qa.a: Abhinav thanked Amma sincerely, bought something needed, and kept the rest for her birthday gift.

qa.q: How did Amma feel receiving the jasmine gajra?
qa.a: Touched and happy; she laughed and cried at the same time 🤍

grounding: A child who feels grown up getting pocket money comes to appreciate the parent's hard work behind it and spends thoughtfully.

passage:
From Mehak's family notebook, Sunday.
Today Divyansh got his first weekly pocket money, a fifty-rupee note, and walked around the flat holding it like a certificate. 'I'm grown up now,' he announced. By evening he had counted it eleven times. On the way to the market with his father, he stopped at the toy stall, then at the samosa cart, then put the note back in his pocket. At dinner he asked, 'Papa, how many hours do you work for fifty rupees?' His father told him honestly. Divyansh went quiet. Later he told me he had decided to buy a birthday card for his grandmother and keep the rest in his tin until he knew what he really wanted. He said, 'Thank you for the money, Mummy,' twice.

qa.q: How many times did Divyansh count the note?
How did Divyansh feel holding his first pocket money?
qa.a: Proud and grown up, holding it like a certificate.

qa.q: What did Divyansh's question to Papa lead to?
qa.a: He understood the work behind the money, thanked his parents, and chose carefully what to spend it on.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt answering Divyansh's question?
qa.a: Pleased that Divyansh was curious about the effort behind the money.

grounding: A mother's notebook records her son's first pocket money, his pride, and his growing gratitude for the work behind it.
